title: Given a Scenario, Configure Basic Mobile Device Network Connectivity and Provide Application Support

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A mobile device can have working hardware and still fail the user if it cannot connect, pair, locate itself, access managed company resources, or synchronize information.
This objective covers five connected areas: wireless and cellular connectivity, Bluetooth pairing, location services, mobile device management, and synchronization.
bullets: Wireless/cellular data network: 3G, 4G, 5G, hotspot, Wi-Fi, SIM, and eSIM
Bluetooth: enable, pair, authenticate, and test nearby devices
Location services: GPS and cellular location services
Mobile device management (MDM): corporate/BYOD configurations, policy enforcement, and corporate applications
Mobile device synchronization: data caps, calendar, contacts, mail, and cloud storage

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a mobile user cannot reach a network, pair an accessory, use location features, access managed resources, or synchronize data, can you identify the layer that should be investigated?
bullets: Internet or network path → Cellular data or Wi-Fi

sections.title: Wireless and Cellular Data Networks
paragraphs: A mobile device can access networks through carrier-provided cellular service or a local Wi-Fi network. Enable or disable the appropriate path based on coverage, user needs, data usage, troubleshooting, and security requirements.
The first question is: which network is the device supposed to be using?
sections.callout: Cellular data and Wi-Fi are separate paths; disabling one does not remove internet access when the other remains connected.

sections.title: 3G, 4G, and 5G
paragraphs: 3G, 4G, and 5G represent successive generations of cellular network technology. Recognize the progression rather than treating each label as a guaranteed speed.
Actual performance depends on carrier, coverage, signal strength, device support, and congestion.

table.caption: Cellular generation recognition
rows: Later generation with improved mobile-data capability
Newer generation designed for greater performance and capacity

sections.callout: Internet through a mobile carrier instead of a local wireless LAN → cellular data.

sections.title: Wi-Fi and Hotspot

entries.title: Wi-Fi
paragraphs: Wi-Fi connects a mobile device to a local wireless network. Enable Wi-Fi, select the intended network, enter the required credentials, and verify connectivity.
entries.memoryHook: Wi-Fi joins the local wireless LAN.
entries.recognitionCue: A phone or tablet must join an existing local wireless network → Wi-Fi.

entries.title: Hotspot
paragraphs: A hotspot lets a mobile device share its network connection with another device. A common setup shares the phone's cellular data by presenting a Wi-Fi network that a laptop joins.
entries.memoryHook: The phone becomes the Wi-Fi source.
entries.recognitionCue: The laptop has no internet, but the phone has cellular data → enable hotspot.

sections.callout: Wi-Fi joins; hotspot shares. Hotspot activity may consume the phone's cellular data allowance.

sections.title: SIM and eSIM
paragraphs: A Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) supplies subscriber information for cellular service. A traditional SIM is a removable physical module; an eSIM provides supported SIM functionality electronically.

table.caption: SIM vs. eSIM
rows: Physical module inserted into a compatible device

sections.callout: Physical subscriber module → SIM. Cellular activation without inserting a card → eSIM.

sections.title: Bluetooth
paragraphs: Bluetooth provides short-range wireless communication with nearby compatible devices such as headsets, earbuds, speakers, keyboards, and mice.
For this objective, know not only what Bluetooth is but also how to establish and verify a connection.

sections.title: Bluetooth Pairing Process
bullets: Enable Bluetooth on the mobile device.
Enable pairing or discoverable mode on the accessory.
Find the device by scanning for available Bluetooth devices.
Enter or confirm the appropriate personal identification number (PIN) code when required.
Test connectivity by using the accessory's intended function.
sections.callout: ON → PAIR → FIND → PIN → TEST. Connected is not finished until the function is verified.

sections.title: Bluetooth Enabled vs. Pairing Enabled
paragraphs: Bluetooth enabled means the wireless function is turned on. Pairing enabled means a device is ready to establish a new Bluetooth relationship.
An accessory can remain invisible even when the phone's Bluetooth is on because the accessory was not placed in pairing or discoverable mode.
sections.callout: The accessory does not appear during discovery → check pairing mode.

sections.title: Location Services
paragraphs: Mobile applications use location services for navigation, maps, tracking, nearby information, and other location-aware features. This objective distinguishes GPS services from cellular location services.

entries.title: GPS Services
paragraphs: Global Positioning System (GPS) uses satellite signals to determine geographic position and is strongly associated with navigation.

entries.title: Cellular Location Services
paragraphs: Cellular location uses information from mobile network infrastructure to help estimate a device's location.
entries.recognitionCue: Location based on cellular infrastructure → cellular location services.

sections.callout: Sky → GPS. Towers → cellular location. Modern devices may combine methods.

sections.title: Mobile Device Management (MDM)
paragraphs: Mobile device management (MDM) lets an organization centrally manage mobile devices and protect company information accessed from phones and tablets.
MDM can manage device configurations, enforce policies, and control corporate applications across a mobile fleet.
sections.callout: An organization needs centralized configuration and control of mobile devices → MDM.

sections.title: Corporate Devices vs. BYOD

entries.title: Corporate Device Configuration
paragraphs: A corporate device is owned and managed by the organization. MDM can apply required configurations consistently across company-owned devices.
entries.recognitionCue: The organization owns the hardware → corporate configuration.

entries.title: Bring Your Own Device (BYOD)
paragraphs: Bring your own device (BYOD) means an employee uses a personally owned phone or tablet to access approved business applications, mail, information, or services.
entries.recognitionCue: The employee owns the device and uses it for company work → BYOD.

sections.callout: Ownership decides the label: company owns it → corporate; employee owns it → BYOD.

entries.title: Policy Enforcement
paragraphs: MDM can centrally apply organizational requirements instead of relying on each user to configure them manually.
entries.recognitionCue: One company rule must apply across many managed devices → policy enforcement.

entries.title: Corporate Applications
paragraphs: MDM can install, configure, manage, or control access to applications required for company work.
entries.recognitionCue: Work applications must be centrally managed on mobile devices → corporate applications.

sections.title: Mobile Device Synchronization
paragraphs: Mobile device synchronization keeps information consistent across devices, applications, or services. A change made on one connected device can appear on another after synchronization.
For this objective, recognize calendar, contacts, mail, cloud storage, and the effect of cellular data caps.
sections.callout: Change it here and see it there → synchronization.

sections.title: Recognizing Data Caps
paragraphs: A data cap limits the amount of cellular data available under a plan. File synchronization, cloud uploads and downloads, and hotspot usage can consume that allowance.
When practical, Wi-Fi can support large synchronization tasks without consuming cellular data.
sections.callout: Large synchronization task plus a limited cellular plan → consider the data cap.

entries.title: Calendar
paragraphs: Calendar synchronization keeps appointments and events consistent across connected devices or services.
entries.recognitionCue: The same meetings must appear on the laptop and phone → calendar synchronization.

entries.title: Contacts
paragraphs: Contact synchronization keeps address-book information consistent across connected devices or accounts.
entries.recognitionCue: The same updated address book is needed across devices → contact synchronization.

sections.title: Business Applications: Mail and Cloud Storage

entries.title: Mail
paragraphs: Mail synchronization keeps business email current on the mobile device. Failure can involve network access, account configuration, application settings, synchronization, or organizational requirements.
entries.recognitionCue: The browser works, but business email does not update → investigate mail synchronization and configuration.

entries.title: Cloud Storage
paragraphs: Cloud storage keeps files on a remote service so authorized devices can access or synchronize them. Large transfers over cellular service can consume significant data.
entries.recognitionCue: The same business files must be available across connected devices → cloud storage synchronization.

sections.title: Connectivity vs. Synchronization
paragraphs: Connectivity asks whether the device can reach the network. Synchronization asks whether a particular application's information is updating correctly.
If a browser works but mail does not update, network connectivity has already been demonstrated. Move toward mail, account, application, synchronization, or organizational configuration.
sections.callout: Internet works does not mean every application is configured and synchronizing correctly.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Join a local wireless network → Wi-Fi
Make an accessory discoverable → Enable pairing
Confirm the accessory functions → Test connectivity
Apply mobile rules centrally → Policy enforcement
Manage work apps centrally → Corporate applications
Appointments → Calendar; address book → Contacts; messages → Mail; files → Cloud storage

sections.title: Objective 1.3 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Several technologies can appear in the same mobile scenario. Determine which layer is failing before selecting a setting or service.

entries.title: Cellular Data vs. Wi-Fi
paragraphs: Carrier service points to cellular data. A local wireless LAN points to Wi-Fi. Either path can provide internet independently.

entries.title: Wi-Fi vs. Hotspot
paragraphs: Wi-Fi joins an existing network. A hotspot lets the mobile device provide connectivity to another device.

entries.title: SIM vs. eSIM
paragraphs: A SIM is a physical subscriber module. An eSIM is electronically provisioned. A cellular generation such as 5G does not determine which one is used.

entries.title: Bluetooth Enabled vs. Pairing Enabled
paragraphs: Bluetooth can be on while an accessory remains undiscoverable. The accessory must enter pairing mode.

entries.title: Pairing vs. Testing
paragraphs: Pairing establishes the connection; testing proves the device performs its intended function.

entries.title: GPS vs. Cellular Location
paragraphs: Satellite source points to GPS; cellular infrastructure points to cellular location services.

entries.title: Corporate vs. BYOD
paragraphs: Ask who owns the hardware: organization means corporate; employee means BYOD.

entries.title: MDM vs. Synchronization
paragraphs: MDM manages and controls devices; synchronization keeps information consistent.

sections.callout: Ask which problem you are solving: CONNECT, PAIR, LOCATE, MANAGE, or SYNC.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Phone supplies internet to another device → Hotspot
Apply company requirements centrally → Policy enforcement
Manage company mobile apps → Corporate applications
Appointments → Calendar; people → Contacts; messages → Mail; files → Cloud storage
